sets.title: Set 2: Practice Questions
sets.description: Practice MCQs (Q1 to Q20) on Trauma and Emergency Care (MSN 102), based on the lecture notes by Joyce Muraguri.

questions.text: A medical emergency is best defined as:

options.A: A sudden injury or serious illness that, if not treated right away, could cause death or serious harm
options.B: A chronic illness that needs regular follow-up
options.C: Any condition that requires admission to hospital
options.D: An injury caused only by a hard or sharp object

questions.explanation: A sudden injury or serious illness that, if not treated right away, could cause death or serious harm (A) is correct because this is the definition of a medical emergency: it is sudden and time-critical, and it is managed by a multidisciplinary team. A chronic illness needing follow-up (B) is not sudden and is not time-critical. Any condition requiring admission (C) is incorrect because many admissions are planned or non-urgent. An injury caused only by a hard or sharp object (D) describes physical trauma, which is only one type of emergency.

questions.text: Which of the following is part of standard precautions that protect both health workers and patients?

options.A: Determining the number of patients at the scene
options.B: Applying a rigid cervical extrication collar
options.C: Safe injections and sharps injury prevention
options.D: Preparing a long backboard and strapping

questions.explanation: Safe injections and sharps injury prevention (C) is correct because standard precautions aim to reduce the risk of transmission of microorganisms from recognised and unrecognised sources, and they include PPE, respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette, safe injections and sharps injury prevention, and chemical suits and gas masks in a toxic environment. Determining the number of patients (A) is part of scene safety. A rigid cervical extrication collar (B) and a long backboard with strapping (D) are extrication equipment that is prepared during scene assessment, not infection-control precautions.

questions.text: Shock is best defined as a clinical syndrome resulting from:

options.A: Failure of the kidneys to excrete waste
options.B: A fall in blood pressure below 120/80 mmHg
options.C: Inadequate tissue perfusion with an imbalance between oxygen delivery and cellular needs

questions.explanation: Inadequate tissue perfusion with an imbalance between oxygen delivery and cellular needs (C) is correct because shock = inadequate tissue perfusion. Normal perfusion needs four intact components: an intact vascular system, adequate fluid volume, adequate air exchange in the lungs, and a functioning heart pump. Kidney failure (A) is a possible complication, not the definition. A blood pressure below 120/80 (B) is not the definition, since the pressure may still be normal in early shock. A fast heart rate (D) is only one sign of shock.

questions.text: In shock, the toxic end product that accumulates in cells because of the shift to anaerobic metabolism is:
questions.explanation: Lactic acid (A) is correct because, when oxygen is lacking, cells switch from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism, which yields little energy and produces lactic acid. Its accumulation causes an acidotic intracellular environment, cell swelling, membrane damage, cell death and the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS). Adenosine triphosphate (B) is the energy store that falls in shock. Glycogen (C) is an energy store, not a toxic by-product. Urea (D) is a waste product of protein metabolism.

questions.text: Which of the following are causes of hypovolemic shock?

options.C: Spinal cord injury and spinal anaesthesia
options.D: Multiple trauma, gastrointestinal haemorrhage and burn injuries

questions.explanation: Multiple trauma, gastrointestinal haemorrhage and burn injuries (D) is correct because hypovolemic shock results from significant loss of blood, plasma or other body fluids; other causes are epistaxis, vaginal haemorrhage, vomiting and excessive diarrhoea. Myocardial infarction and cardiomyopathy (A) cause cardiogenic shock. Pulmonary embolism and cardiac tamponade (B) cause obstructive shock. Spinal cord injury and spinal anaesthesia (C) cause neurogenic (distributive) shock.

questions.text: Which of the following is a LATE sign of hypovolemic shock?

options.C: Mottling of the skin with absent peripheral pulses

questions.explanation: Mottling of the skin with absent peripheral pulses (C) is correct because late signs include cool, clammy, dusky or mottled skin, absent peripheral pulses, hypotension, bradycardia, absent bowel sounds, anuria, central cyanosis, respiratory failure, dilated pupils and unresponsiveness, together with lactic acidosis above 4 mmol/L. Anxiety and restlessness (A), thirst and nausea (B), and tachypnoea and air hunger (D) are early signs, when the body is still compensating.

questions.text: In the management of a patient in hypovolemic shock, the nurse should obtain intravenous access using catheters of at least:
questions.explanation: 16 gauge (A) is correct because large-bore catheters (16 gauge or greater if possible) allow rapid infusion of fluid boluses and blood products. The smaller gauges 22 (B), 20 (C) and 18 (D) have a narrower lumen and a slower flow rate, so they are not suitable for rapid volume resuscitation. Remember that a higher gauge number means a smaller catheter.
questions.sourceRef: Shock: General management of hypovolemic shock

questions.text: A patient has a heart rate of 80 beats per minute and a stroke volume of 70 mL. The cardiac output is:
questions.explanation: 5,600 mL per minute (B) is correct because cardiac output = heart rate x stroke volume: 80 x 70 = 5,600 mL, which is 5.6 litres per minute and is close to the average of about 5 litres per minute in a healthy resting adult. 150 mL (A) is the sum of the two values, not their product. 560 mL (C) and 56,000 mL (D) are errors of decimal place.
questions.sourceRef: Shock: Cardiogenic shock, cardiac output formula

questions.text: In the management of cardiogenic shock, the purpose of positioning the patient in semi-Fowler's or Fowler's position is to:

options.A: Increase venous return to the heart
options.B: Decrease preload and reduce the workload of the heart
options.C: Raise the blood pressure by pooling blood in the legs

questions.explanation: Decrease preload and reduce the workload of the heart (B) is correct because sitting the patient up decreases venous return (preload) to the heart, which minimises cardiac workload; vasodilators such as nitroglycerin and diuretics are used for the same purpose. Increasing venous return (A) would worsen pulmonary congestion in a failing pump. Raising the blood pressure by pooling blood in the legs (C) is not the aim. Preventing aspiration (D) is not the reason for this position in cardiogenic shock.

questions.text: The three categories of distributive shock are:
questions.explanation: Anaphylactic, septic and neurogenic (C) is correct because in distributive shock the intravascular volume pools in peripheral blood vessels, causing a relative hypovolemia, and the three categories are anaphylactic, septic and neurogenic shock. The other options are incorrect because each of them includes hypovolemic, cardiogenic or obstructive shock, which are separate types of shock and are not forms of distributive shock.

questions.text: Mr. K, who weighs 70 kg, develops anaphylaxis after a bee sting. Using 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) epinephrine at 0.01 mg/kg, the dose to be given intramuscularly is:
questions.explanation: 0.7 mL (A) is correct because 0.01 mg/kg x 70 kg = 0.7 mg, and since 1:1,000 epinephrine contains 1 mg in each mL, 0.7 mg is 0.7 mL, given intramuscularly in the mid-anterolateral thigh. The time of administration is documented and the dose may be repeated in 5 to 15 minutes if needed. 0.07 mL (B), 7 mL (C) and 70 mL (D) are errors of decimal place; 7 mL or 70 mL would be a dangerous overdose.

questions.text: Which of the following findings is characteristic of neurogenic shock?

options.C: Bradycardia, hypotension and warm, dry, flushed skin

questions.explanation: Bradycardia, hypotension and warm, dry, flushed skin (C) is correct because loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation, low blood pressure (systolic below 90 mmHg or 30 mmHg below baseline), a reduced heart rate and temperature dysregulation. Tachycardia with cold, clammy skin (A) is typical of hypovolemic shock. Hypertension (B) does not occur in shock. Pink frothy sputum (D) is a sign of pulmonary oedema or near drowning.

questions.text: Septic shock is best described as:

options.A: The least common type of distributive shock
options.B: The most common type of distributive shock and the last and most severe stage of sepsis
options.C: A type of cardiogenic shock caused by infection of the heart
options.D: A type of obstructive shock caused by infected clots

questions.explanation: The most common type of distributive shock and the last and most severe stage of sepsis (B) is correct because septic shock is caused by widespread infection (most commonly by gram-negative bacteria) and is managed with antibiotics, IV fluids, oxygen, low-dose corticosteroids, insulin, anticoagulants and nutritional support. It is not the least common (A). It is a distributive shock, not cardiogenic (C) or obstructive (D).

questions.text: The immediate management of a patient in obstructive shock due to tension pneumothorax is:

options.B: Needle decompression followed by chest tube placement

questions.explanation: Needle decompression followed by chest tube placement (B) is correct because in tension pneumothorax air continuously enters the pleural space and compresses the heart and vessels, so the obstruction must be relieved at once. Pericardiocentesis (A) is for cardiac tamponade. Intravenous anticoagulation (C) is for pulmonary embolism. Dobutamine (D) improves contractility in cardiogenic shock and does not remove the obstruction.

questions.text: In a patient who has swallowed a poison, activated charcoal is most effective when administered within:
questions.explanation: One hour of ingestion (D) is correct because activated charcoal adsorbs toxins in the gastrointestinal tract and prevents their absorption, and it is most effective within one hour, though it may still help up to 4 hours for certain substances. It is given orally or via a nasogastric tube. Six (A), twelve (B) and twenty-four hours (C) are too late, since most of the poison will already have been absorbed. Gastric lavage is likewise useful only within 1 to 4 hours of ingestion.
questions.sourceRef: Poisoning: Activated charcoal and gastric lavage

questions.text: The specific antidote for acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning is:
questions.explanation: Acetylcysteine (D) is correct because it is the antidote for acetaminophen poisoning. Naloxone (A) reverses opioids. Atropine (B) is the antidote for organophosphorus compounds. Fomepizole (C) is used for methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.text: Which of the following should the nurse AVOID when giving first aid for a snake bite?

options.A: Applying a tourniquet above the bite
options.B: Immobilising the bitten limb, preferably with a splint
options.C: Cleaning the wound under running water
options.D: Removing jewellery and tight clothing near the bite

questions.explanation: Applying a tourniquet above the bite (A) is correct because after a snake bite one should avoid tourniquets, cutting the wound, applying ice and sucking the wound. Immobilising the limb (B) slows the circulation of venom. Cleaning the wound under running water (C) reduces the venom on the skin. Removing jewellery and tight clothing (D) is done because swelling will follow, and constricting items could cut off the circulation.

questions.text: A patient is admitted after a near-drowning incident. The patient is admitted for at least 24 hours of observation because of the risk of:
questions.explanation: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) (A) is correct because aspiration of even 1 to 3 mL/kg of water alters surfactant function and interferes with gas exchange, and contaminants such as mud, algae and chlorine increase lung damage; dyspnoea may worsen over several hours, so the patient is observed for a minimum of 24 hours. Hypertension (B), hyperglycaemia (C) and cerebral malaria (D) are not the recognised complications of drowning that justify the observation period.

questions.text: The three components of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT) are:

options.D: General appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin

questions.explanation: General appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin (D) is correct because the PAT is the quick 'critical look' used as the first step in assessing a child, to form a general impression and to decide the severity of illness or injury and the urgency of the intervention. Airway, breathing and circulation (A) is the ABC approach, which is not the PAT. Pulse, blood pressure and temperature (B) are vital signs, and the PAT is done without touching the child. Alert, voice and pain (C) is part of the AVPU scale.

questions.text: In the primary survey, the 'D' (disability) interventions in a patient with a head injury include:

options.A: Keeping the patient flat with the head down
options.B: Maintaining systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg and SpO2 above 90%
options.C: Giving high volumes of fluid to keep the systolic pressure above 140 mmHg
options.D: Increasing external stimuli to keep the patient awake

questions.explanation: Maintaining systolic blood pressure above 100 mmHg and SpO2 above 90% (B) is correct because these targets protect cerebral perfusion and oxygenation; other interventions are elevating the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees (if there is no spinal injury or once stabilised), preparing to give mannitol for changes in consciousness linked to raised intracranial pressure, and decreasing external stimuli. Keeping the patient flat with the head down (A) would raise intracranial pressure. Giving large volumes of fluid for a pressure above 140 (C) is not recommended. Increasing external stimuli (D) is incorrect because stimuli should be decreased.

questions.text: A multidisciplinary team in emergency care is best described as:

options.A: A group of nurses of the same specialty working on one shift
options.B: A team that includes only doctors and nurses
options.C: A team that is formed only during disasters
options.D: A group of professionals from different specialties who collaborate to achieve a common goal in the care of a complex patient

questions.explanation: A group of professionals from different specialties who collaborate to achieve a common goal in the care of a complex patient (D) is correct; the emergency nurse is part of this team and each member contributes his or her own expertise. A group of nurses of the same specialty (A) is not multidisciplinary. A team of only doctors and nurses (B) is too narrow, because other professionals are also included. A team formed only in disasters (C) is incorrect because emergencies are managed by such teams every day.
questions.sourceRef: Definition of terms: Emergency, multidisciplinary team

questions.text: Which of the following is an example of blunt force trauma?

options.B: A victim hit by a hard object

questions.explanation: A victim hit by a hard object (B) is correct because blunt force trauma occurs when a victim hits or is hit by a hard object, producing contusions, abrasions and lacerations. A stab (A), a cut by glass (C) and a puncture by a nail (D) are examples of sharp-force trauma, where the victim is poked, cut or stabbed by something sharp; when an object pierces the body, usually creating an open wound, it is called penetrating trauma.

questions.text: According to the epidemiology of trauma deaths, the first peak of death, occurring within seconds or minutes of injury, results from:

options.B: Lacerations of the heart, large vessels, brain or spinal cord
options.D: Uncontrolled haemorrhage from a pelvic fracture

questions.explanation: Lacerations of the heart, large vessels, brain or spinal cord (B) is correct because these injuries are so severe that death occurs within seconds or minutes. Sepsis (A) causes the third peak, days to weeks after injury, together with multi-organ failure and respiratory complications. Intracranial haematoma (C) and uncontrolled haemorrhage from pelvic fractures, solid organ lacerations or multiple wounds (D) cause the second peak, minutes to hours after the injury.

questions.text: Before approaching a patient at an accident scene, the emergency nurse should first assess scene safety, which is defined as:

options.A: Rapid sorting of casualties by priority
options.B: A head-to-toe examination of the casualty
options.C: Assessment and management of the environment to identify and prevent hazards before providing care, to protect oneself, other responders and bystanders

questions.explanation: Assessment and management of the environment to identify and prevent hazards before providing care, to protect oneself, other responders and bystanders (C) is correct because this is the definition of scene safety; it also includes determining the number of patients and the equipment needed for extrication, such as a cervical collar, long backboard, oxygen and airway equipment with suction and a bag-valve mask, and a trauma bag. Rapid sorting of casualties (A) is triage. A head-to-toe examination (B) is the secondary survey. Cervical spine immobilisation (D) is part of airway management in the primary survey.

questions.text: A 20 kg child is in hypovolemic shock. Using the normal saline bolus of 10 mL/kg, the volume to be given rapidly is:
questions.explanation: 200 mL (B) is correct because the paediatric bolus is 10 mL/kg, so 10 x 20 = 200 mL, given rapidly over 5 to 20 minutes. In adults the bolus is 500 to 1,000 mL. 20 mL (A) and 100 mL (C) are too small to restore circulating volume. 1,000 mL (D) is the adult dose and would overload a child. Other measures in hypovolemic shock are to control bleeding, give high-flow oxygen, prevent hypothermia, and insert a gastric tube to reduce gastric distension, which is associated with vomiting and aspiration.

questions.text: Which of the following laboratory findings is consistent with early hypovolemic shock?
questions.explanation: Serum lactate above 2 mmol/L (B) is correct because poor perfusion causes anaerobic metabolism, and early signs include a mean arterial pressure below 60 mmHg and a raised serum lactate above 2 mmol/L. Later, the lactic acidosis exceeds 4 mmol/L and the base deficit is worse than -4 mmol/L. A lactate below 1 mmol/L (A) and an MAP above 90 mmHg (C) are normal. A base excess above +4 (D) is not found in shock, where a base deficit develops.

questions.text: Which of the following is a cause of cardiogenic shock?
questions.explanation: Dysrhythmias and valvular disease (D) is correct because cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart's ability to contract and pump is impaired; causes include ventricular ischaemia, myocardial infarction, dysrhythmias, cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, recent chest trauma, and medications such as beta-blockers. Excessive diarrhoea (A) causes hypovolemic shock. Spinal anaesthesia (B) causes neurogenic shock. Pulmonary embolism (C) causes obstructive shock.

questions.text: In the management of anaphylaxis, the nurse should know that antihistamine therapy is:

options.A: The first-line treatment, given before epinephrine
options.D: Given instead of fluids in hypotension

questions.explanation: An adjunct to epinephrine administration (C) is correct because epinephrine is the first-line treatment and antihistamines are only added afterwards. Other measures are high-flow oxygen by non-rebreather mask at 10 to 15 L/min, IV access, removing the causative agent, a rapid infusion of 1 to 2 L of 0.9% saline for hypotension (5 to 10 mL/kg in the first 5 to 10 minutes), and inhaled beta-2 agonists such as albuterol for bronchospasm. Antihistamines are not first-line (A), are not contraindicated (B), and do not replace fluids (D).

questions.text: The most common cause of neurogenic shock is:
questions.explanation: Spinal cord injury (D) is correct because it is the most common cause; the injury interrupts the sympathetic impulses that keep blood vessels in a state of partial constriction, so they dilate. Deep general anaesthesia (A), spinal anaesthesia, brain damage (C) and toxins (B) are also causes, but are less common. Management is directed at the ABCs, vasopressors such as norepinephrine to constrict the vasculature, and atropine if the heart rate needs to be raised.

questions.text: In the management of septic shock, low-dose corticosteroids such as hydrocortisone are given because:

options.C: Patients in septic shock have adrenal insufficiency and need adrenal support

questions.explanation: Patients in septic shock have adrenal insufficiency and need adrenal support (C) is correct. Antibiotics (A) kill the bacteria. Anticoagulants such as heparin (B) limit unneeded clotting and prevent consumption of clotting factors. Insulin therapy (D) lowers the blood sugar, because sepsis speeds up glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and reduces tissue glucose uptake, causing hyperglycaemia that worsens outcomes. Nutritional therapy is also started within 24 to 48 hours to meet the hypermetabolic state.

questions.text: Mr. P presents with muffled heart sounds after a stab wound to the chest, and blood fills the sac around his heart, stopping it from pumping. The immediate treatment is:
questions.explanation: Pericardiocentesis (D) is correct because cardiac tamponade is an obstructive shock in which excess blood or fluid fills the pericardial sac, so it must be drained immediately, followed by surgical intervention for cardiac repair. Needle decompression (A) is for tension pneumothorax. Thrombolytics (B) are used in selected cases of pulmonary embolism. Diuretics (C) reduce volume and would worsen the obstruction to ventricular filling.

questions.text: Which of the following is the correct first aid for poisoning by the stated route?

options.A: Skin or eyes: rinse with water for at least 15 to 20 minutes and remove contaminated clothing
options.D: Skin or eyes: apply a neutralising solution

questions.explanation: Skin or eyes: rinse with water for at least 15 to 20 minutes and remove contaminated clothing (A) is correct. If the poison was inhaled, the person is moved to fresh air at once (B is incorrect). If it was ingested, vomiting must not be induced (C is incorrect). A neutralising solution (D) is not recommended, because it can cause a further chemical reaction. The nurse should also try to identify the substance, the amount and the time.

questions.text: An adult with suspected chronic alcohol abuse presents with agitation and seizures. The appropriate drugs include:

options.D: Thiamine 50 to 100 mg IV and a benzodiazepine such as diazepam

questions.explanation: Thiamine 50 to 100 mg IV and a benzodiazepine such as diazepam (D) is correct because chronic alcoholics are at high risk of vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency, and benzodiazepines are given for agitation and seizures. Atropine and protamine (A) are antidotes for organophosphates and heparin. Naloxone and vitamin K (B) are antidotes for opioids and warfarin. Deferoxamine and glucagon (C) are antidotes for iron and beta-blockers. Blood glucose should also be checked, and dextrose 50% 50 mL IV given if it is low.

questions.text: Which of the following poison and antidote pairs is correct?
questions.explanation: Iron: deferoxamine (C) is correct. Heparin (A) is reversed by protamine sulfate, not vitamin K. Warfarin (B) is reversed by vitamin K, not protamine sulfate. Cyanide (D) is treated with hydroxocobalamin, while methylene blue is for methemoglobinemia. Other pairs: lead, arsenic and mercury with EDTA, dimercaprol and penicillamine; magnesium sulfate with calcium gluconate; and beta-blockers with glucagon.

questions.text: A patient is brought in unresponsive with pinpoint pupils and slow breathing after a suspected opioid overdose. The nurse should prepare to give naloxone at a dose of:
questions.explanation: 0.4 to 2 mg (C) is correct because for potential opioid exposure naloxone (Narcan) is given in a dose of 0.4 to 2 mg, intravenously, via endotracheal tube, intramuscularly, subcutaneously, intraosseously or sublingually. 10 to 20 mg (A) and 50 to 100 mg (B) are excessive (50 to 100 mg is the dose of thiamine). 0.01 mg/kg of 1:1,000 (D) is the dose of epinephrine for anaphylaxis.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about snake bites is correct?

options.A: Bites to the head or trunk are often more severe than bites to the extremities
options.B: Dry bites cannot occur because every bite injects venom
options.C: Antivenin is given for every snake bite
options.D: The patient is observed for only 1 hour

questions.explanation: Bites to the head or trunk are often more severe than bites to the extremities (A) is correct; other factors in severity are snake size and species, the amount of venom injected, the age, size and health of the patient, the time to treatment and individual susceptibility. A dry bite (B) delivers no venom, so it can occur. Antivenin (C) is not used for mild or resolving symptoms; it is indicated for progressive pain, swelling or ecchymosis, and since it is made from animal serum it can cause life-threatening allergic reactions. The patient is monitored for at least 6 hours (D) to decide whether antivenin is needed.
questions.sourceRef: Snake bites: Severity and hospital management

questions.text: In drowning, the nurse should know that in 10% to 20% of cases:

options.A: The patient aspirates more than 4 litres of water
options.B: Laryngospasm prevents the aspiration of water

questions.explanation: Laryngospasm prevents the aspiration of water (B) is correct; where aspiration does occur the amount is usually less than 4 mL/kg, and as little as 1 to 3 mL/kg can alter surfactant function. Aspiration of 4 litres (A) is not the usual amount. Core temperature must be checked and the patient warmed as needed (C is incorrect). The faster resuscitation is started and the hypoxia, hypercarbia and acidosis are corrected, the better the chance of survival (D is incorrect). A gastric tube is inserted to decompress the stomach.

questions.text: On the Pediatric Assessment Triangle, which finding under 'work of breathing' is ABNORMAL?

options.A: Nasal flaring, retractions and tracheal tug
options.C: Good muscle tone and normal cry
options.D: Capillary refill of 2 seconds or less

questions.explanation: Nasal flaring, retractions and tracheal tug (A) is correct because abnormal work of breathing includes increased effort, nasal flaring, retractions, abdominal muscle use, noisy breathing, and decreased or absent respiratory effort. Quiet, easy, unlabored breathing (B) is normal. Good muscle tone and a normal cry (C) are normal general appearance. A capillary refill of 2 seconds or less (D) is a normal circulation-to-skin finding.

questions.text: During the primary survey, which airway intervention is CONTRAINDICATED in a patient with facial trauma?

options.D: Insertion of an oropharyngeal airway in an unconscious patient

questions.explanation: Insertion of a nasopharyngeal airway (A) is correct because a nasopharyngeal airway must never be inserted in patients with facial trauma. The jaw thrust (B) is used in trauma because it opens the airway without moving the neck, and cervical spine immobilisation is done at the same time. Suctioning loose objects, teeth and secretions (C) is part of airway care. An oropharyngeal airway (D) is used in an unconscious patient with no gag reflex.

questions.text: The secondary survey differs from the primary survey in that it:

options.A: Is done before any life-saving interventions
options.B: Deals only with airway and breathing
options.C: Is done only once and never repeated
options.D: Is a systematic head-to-toe examination done after life-saving interventions, and includes a full set of vital signs as a baseline

questions.explanation: Is a systematic head-to-toe examination done after life-saving interventions, and includes a full set of vital signs as a baseline (D) is correct; it also includes history taking, laboratory and radiological investigations, and other interventions such as wound dressing, splinting and tetanus prophylaxis. In suspected chest trauma, apical and radial pulses are documented and blood pressure is taken in both arms because of the risk of aortic trauma. It is done after, not before, life-saving interventions (A). It covers the whole body, not only A and B (B). The patient is re-evaluated regularly to identify deterioration and missed injuries, and documentation is essential (C).
